articles.title: US Agencies Propose Cyber Controls for Frontier AI Systems
articles.content: The federal government is advising AI companies to set more industry standards for securing agents in sandbox testing environments. In joint guidance from the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, the National Security Agency and the Center for Advancing Innovation and Standards for Super Intelligence (CAISSI) at the Department of Commerce, AI companies are encouraged to lean more heavily on cybersecurity technical controls, independent testing and evaluation of new models and develop “shut down policies” that govern when a model or test should be taken offline. The guidance comes after a summer when OpenAI , Anthropic , Google , Meta and other companies say their AI models escaped from testing environments and hacked real organizations and websites. The problem has bedeviled frontier AI companies, with many of their own researchers saying it’s possible that hundreds – even thousands – of similar sandbox escapes may have occurred over the summer, raising major questions about the lack of effective monitoring in place. “While these incidents highlight the importance of traditional cybersecurity principles and practices, they also introduce novel considerations for incident prevention, response, and reporting,” the agencies wrote. “These novel considerations primarily stem from the agentic nature and advanced cyber capabilities of cutting-edge SI systems.” While voluntary, the document marks the federal government’s most detailed cybersecurity guidance for securing sandbox environments during AI model tests.  The first set of recommendations deals with designing and implementing technical controls for the virtualized testing environments, while another recommends outside monitoring tools to ensure AI models don’t access tools or privileges they shouldn’t have. Cybersecurity experts have said both features were lacking in the testing environments used by AI companies this past summer. AI testers must also scour their internal testing environments for “potential persistence mechanisms and unauthorized communication across internal and external systems” that could be used by AI agents to leave notes and collaborate on tasks in secret. It specifically cautions against relying solely on other AI systems to monitor and restrain the behavior of their test models, using the government’s now-preferred term of “Super Intelligence” or “SI.” “Test and red-team SI control measures with humans and SI systems before deploying them,” the guidance states. “Only use SI systems to red-team in cases where out-of-scope actions could not result in harm to critical systems.” Security teams must evaluate risk not only from the large language model, but also from the surrounding systems and infrastructure it relies on, like the technical harness , the host and broader network, and each layer has security protocols that can stop unauthorized access to the internet or detect anomalous behavior. Another recommendation calls for frontier AI companies to be more open to partnering with “independent, external auditors” to assess their controls and monitoring for AI agent testing. Critics have argued that Anthropic and OpenAI rely too heavily on a small group of little-known nonprofits and private research organizations, like METR and Redwood Research, to test their frontier models for safety and security concerns and respond to incidents like the Hugging Face hack. They question why these companies don’t work with more established cybersecurity or incident response firms. Chris Painter, METR’s president, told Congress earlier this month that it had become industry practice for frontier companies to rely almost entirely on other AI systems to monitor and restrain their models in testing environments, citing the sheer volume of data and telemetry that researchers must sift through. Cybersecurity and AI experts have told CyberScoop that a combination of human oversight, technical controls and AI systems is the most effective means of restraining the kind of agent hacks that have consumed the news. The guidance further calls for executive leadership at these companies to be more personally involved in decisions around pausing or restarting a particular project, and only after they’ve been informed of the relevant potential risks.

This guidance aims to mitigate the inherent risks associated with advanced AI, from data poisoning and adversarial attacks to misuse by malicious actors. The recommendations signal a coordinated governmental effort to establish a baseline for AI security, acknowledging that current practices are insufficient for these powerful and rapidly evolving technologies.

articles.title: Trump, Musk Deny Starlink Interference in Ukraine
articles.content: LivestreamMenuPresident Trump denied that the White House had ordered restrictions on SpaceX's Starlink satellite internet services in Ukraine this week.Ukrainian officials complained on Tuesday and Wednesday that SpaceX had limited internet connectivity via Starshield without advance notice.Musk said any restrictions on Starlink or Starshield in Ukraine would have come from decisions by the president or White House. In this article President Donald Trump on Friday denied that the White House had ordered restrictions this week on Starlink satellite internet services provided to Ukraine's armed forces. Ukrainian officials on Tuesday and Wednesday said SpaceX had restricted use of Starshield, a military-grade version of Starlink, without warning, impeding some military operations and its ability to defend civilians against intensifying attacks by Russia. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk pinned responsibility for any restrictions on the U.S. government and Trump, writing on X that, "Starshield systems are owned and controlled by the US government." Reporters in Washington, D.C., on Friday asked Trump who was responsible for pausing access for the Ukrainian military. "Well, I don't know if it was anybody because it wasn't me, and I don't think it was Elon," Trump said. "And from what I understand, it's the same as it's always been." Ukrainian forces have long relied on Starlink and Starshield to enable data gathering by their autonomous drones and for other communications. The restrictions cut off connectivity for drones or other vehicles traveling above 160 kilometers per hour. Serhii Beskrestnov, an advisor to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, wrote in a post on Telegram this week that, "Our armed forces did not receive a warning about these restrictions, and this led to the failure of a number of missions." Radoslaw Sikorski, Poland's deputy prime minister, criticized Musk on X about the restrictions. Poland has purchased Starlink services for Ukraine from SpaceX. "Hey, @elonmusk, big man, are you playing politics with your products again?" he wrote. "As your European customers, we are watching you." Musk is an advisor to the Pentagon on technology through his role in the recently announced Project Meridian. The Telegraph reported Friday that Musk "approached Donald Trump with the idea of slowing down Starlink in Ukraine," and both had a hand in imposing the restrictions. Reuters reported on Thursday, citing two U.S. officials, that the call to restrict Starlink in Ukraine came from the White House, but did not say who made the order. On Oct. 10, after Trump called on Ukraine to stop all attacks on Russian oil refineries, Musk wrote in a post on X, "Zelensky has gone too far." Musk and SpaceX did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Friday. SpaceX shares are down about 11% this week. The company is scheduled to report quarterly results on Tuesday.

articles.title: New York House Race Becomes Referendum on Tech's Influence
articles.content: The Democratic Socialists of America (DSA) candidates running for the House of Representatives and endorsed by NYC Mayor Zohran Mamdani are all but guaranteed to win their general elections this November, but that does not mean the midterm drama is over in New York. In the state's 17th congressional district, which includes the lower Hudson Valley, Democratic challenger Cait Conley, a combat veteran who served on the Biden administration's National Security Council, could unseat incumbent Republican congressman Mike Lawler in one of the most consequential races of the midterms. The highly contested purple district voted for former Vice President Kamala Harris in the 2024 election while reelecting Lawler for his second term. Now, Lawler is attempting to win a third term as support for President Donald Trump wanes ahead of the midterms. As of Friday, The Cook Political Report lists the race, which could determine control of the House, as a toss-up . If elected, Conley would have far more in common with the " Badass Women " coalition of security state and military veterans than with DSA types (think more Sen. Elissa Slotkin from Michigan than Darializa Avila Chevalier ). As Judge Street Journal 's Timmy Facciola notes, "Conley's candidacy is testing the viability of a tactful centrism that rebukes left-wing positions like abolishing ICE or restricting weapon shipments to Israel." Lawler is also vying for moderates, pitching himself as "one of the most bipartisan members of Congress" and emphasizing his willingness to break with Trump occasionally while still welcoming Trump's support. While Lawler and Conley certainly are not pure MAGA acolytes or DSA members, both have leaned into a tech-critical position, much like that of more radical populists like Lina Khan or Steve Bannon , revealing how pervasive anti-tech sentiment has become in mainstream politics. This tech skepticism was on full display during an October 14 debate, when each candidate made the case for why they were the most equipped to regulate AI, insisting that the industry needs guardrails. Conley said members of Congress do not want to regulate AI because "they want to look out for their billionaire and trillionaire backers like Elon Musk, who is pouring over $260 million into this midterm election." She then added that Musk backed Lawler in his 2024 race. Lawler then accused Conley, who previously consulted for Primer AI , of being "the AI candidate for the AI industry." While Lawler and Conley disagree on specific data center regulations (Conley supports Democratic Gov. Kathy Hochul's data center moratorium while Lawler supports local zoning control over data centers), neither wants to pitch themselves as an explicitly pro-data center candidate. During the debate, Conley claimed that, "On Mike Lawler's watch there have been five data centers built in Rockland County." Lawler has said that he had no say in the decision to build the data centers, and during the debate, he pointed out that the facilities were built for financial services . Lawler also attempted to attack Conley over data centers, slamming her in an ad for saying "we need data centers." Regardless of the candidates' specific policies on data centers, their attacks on one another demonstrate that cheerleading hyperscale data center development is a political liability. In their district, data center has presumably become a dirty term. The candidates' tech-skeptical rhetoric did not end with unchecked data center development. After the debate, Reason asked both candidates about their positions on age-verification laws for social media and AI, since such regulations raise significant privacy and censorship concerns by age-gating the internet. Unsurprisingly, both Lawler, who voted for the controversial KIDS Act , and Conley, who has proposed stricter age verification for AI tools, parroted platitudes about why such online safety regulations are necessary to protect children. "We have watched how social media is literally hurting the mental health of children," Conley told Reason . "And when you talk about the power of AI and what that power could do, we have to regulate this." Lawler gave a similar response, telling Reason that he respects free speech but that protecting children "is paramount." This bipartisan consensus over social media regulation has long been brewing in Congress. The mainstream political conversations about AI and data centers, however, are relatively new this midterm election cycle. And it appears both Lawler and Conley have figured out which way Americans' sentiment toward AI is leaning, and they have waged their campaigns accordingly.

articles.title: Delhi Police Facial Recognition Tender: Mass Surveillance Expansion
articles.content: Access the copies of the documents: Request for Proposal | GeM bid document | Technical specifications In July 2026, Delhi Police invited bids for 338 CCTV cameras across its Central and New Delhi districts. The specifications require facial recognition on fixed and pan-tilt-zoom (PTZ) cameras, alongside analytics to detect crowds, abandoned objects and vehicle number plates, according to the tender documents reviewed by MediaNama. The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) first reported on these tender documents. The request for proposal (RFP) , issued by the office of the Additional Commissioner of Police (Provisioning & Logistics), says the cameras are meant “to cover VIP/VVIP route & other locations” for the Republic Day and Independence Day celebrations. Delhi Police estimated the tender’s value at Rs 15.66 crore. The bidding process closed on August 20. The documents reveal that Delhi Police intends to equip every type of camera with facial recognition capabilities: Fixed cameras must include analytics for “Intrusion, Tripwire, People counting/people gathering, face recognition, Tamper detection”. PTZ cameras must include “Tripwire, Intrusion, Object Abandon/Missing, Motion Detection, Face Recognition, Tamper detection”. Automatic number plate recognition (ANPR) cameras , designed to recognise vehicle number plates, must also have edge analytics for “Face Detection”, alongside people counting and gathering, perimeter protection and tamper detection. Video management software (VMS) must also “support Face Recognition System”. The system “should become part of VMS with perpetual license”. The documents also state: “The Manufacturer shall offer a mobile application with the capability to access live video from up to 500 cameras in both iOS and Android/OS platforms.” The documents specify the following locations for the cameras: Ramlila Maidan gate Turkman Gate Delhi Gate Rajghat India Gate hexagon Mandi House Patiala House The RFP states: “CCTV cameras are to be strategically placed at suitable height with structure arrangement, so as to identy and capture the face of a particular person roaming around at Critical/vulnerable points.” For context, a new round of protests began at Jantar Mantar, seeking accountability from the Election Commission of India. The Delhi Police Commissioner de-notified Jantar Mantar as a protest site and designated Ramlila Maidan and two other as a new protest site. Why it matters: The Indian state continues to use and misuse surveillance technology . Yet, no specific statutory law authorises and regulates the police’s use of facial recognition. For instance, Delhi Police has not disclosed the legal framework or safeguards governing its use of facial recognition. As MediaNama reported , the standing order that IFF obtained through a Right to Information (RTI) application does not mention facial recognition at all. The Ministry of Home Affairs cited this order in Parliament when asked about safeguards governing facial recognition. The RFP mentions the word “privacy” only once, in the context of “privacy masking”. This refers to a function that blurs or blacks out selected regions, faces or bodies in live or recorded video footage. In the context of this RFP, “privacy masking 4 area” might mean that each camera must be capable of defining up to four independent privacy zones within its field of view. Each zone could be selectively blurred, blacked out or pixelated to protect private spaces, such as neighbouring windows and balconies, while the rest of the scene remains visible for surveillance. We found no references to privacy, the Digital Personal Data Protection Act or the Puttaswamy judgment in the RFP. IFF also noted this absence. The RFP sets no accuracy standard for facial recognition and does not specify a database against which faces would be matched. It also sets no similarity threshold, rules on who can conduct searches, or retention period for facial data. These details could be covered by another product, framework or workflow and specified in a separate tender. The RFP is primarily a product requirements document, rather than a legal document that sets limits on how the technology can be used or misused. However, the requirements should still address these issues, given that they will shape the system eventually built or delivered. If privacy safeguards are not a priority at the product specification stage, how can we expect the resulting products and services to uphold privacy-preserving principles? Surveillance technology also has real-world consequences. In August 2026, following the July protests at Jantar Mantar, Delhi Police told the Supreme Court in an affidavit that its facial recognition system had identified 2,873 people with criminal antecedents at the protest site between July 20 and 26. Later, The Indian Express found that at least 25 of them were in jail at the time. Integration with Safe City, which includes predictive policing: The RFP requires the cameras to be “compatible to integrate with any other CCTV cameras installed in other projects of Delhi Police like Safe City Project”. The Delhi Police standing order states that the Safe City system “will have tools for predictive policing”, according to IFF . Also read: What remains unanswered from Delhi Police’s RTI reply on live CCTV surveillance & facial recognition Can The DPDP Act Protect Citizens From CCTV Surveillance? articles.title: Norwegian Teen Jailed for UK Murder Plot After Online Recruitment
articles.content: Oct 16, 2026 Add AL-MONITOR on Google An undated handout photo of Johannes Natland released by the Metropolitan Police — Metropolitan Police LONDON, Oct 16 (Reuters) - A Norwegian teenager who flew to Britain to commit murder after being recruited online by a Swedish organised crime group linked to Iran was jailed on Friday for 20 years. British prosecutors said Johannes Natland, now 19, was recruited by the Foxtrot Network, a Swedish criminal group that pays young people to carry out "violence as a service" on behalf of clients, including the Iranian state. He was convicted in July of conspiracy to murder. Natland had not been told the identity of the person he had agreed to kill in return for a payment of 270,000 Norwegian kroner, around $28,600, prosecutors said. The case was one of a number in recent years involving young adults who have stood trial in Britain over serious criminal acts carried out after being recruited online. Britain says some of them have ended up acting as unwitting proxies for foreign states such as Iran or Russia. Foxtrot has been linked to several murders across Europe, and Britain and the US allege the group was behind attacks against Israeli and Jewish targets on behalf of Iran, which denies the allegation. TEEN SAID 'IT WILL BE COOL TO KILL' Natland had only just turned 18 when he flew from Norway to Britain, having responded to an advert which offered money to kill and said "nothing can go wrong". He admitted possessing a semi-automatic pistol, a revolver and ammunition, but denied conspiracy to murder, saying he did not intend to carry out the plan and had considered shooting himself in the foot to get out of it. But prosecutors said Natland was an enthusiastic recruit, who boasted to a friend that "it will be cool to kill someone". Natland was sentenced at London's Woolwich Crown Court to detention for 20 years by Judge Bobbie Cheema-Grubb, who said she was sure he would have carried out the murder if he had not been arrested by police. "This was not an impulsive act lasting a few moments ... your conduct demonstrated purpose and persistence," she said, adding that Natland would serve at least 13 years in custody. Natland's Norwegian lawyer Farid Bouras said in a statement: "Our priority now is to bring him home. We will be working to secure his transfer to Norway as quickly as we possibly can." Commander Helen Flanagan, head of Counter Terrorism Policing London, said there was no evidence of any direct link to Iran in Natland's case, which served as a warning to those who may be recruited to become criminal proxies. "As Natland found, the people orchestrating these crimes will not protect you from the consequences," she said. articles.title: Apple's iPhone Duo Tests Status-Symbol Power at $1,999
articles.content: LivestreamMenuApple's iPhone Duo launch-day pickup inventory sold out quickly, with some delivery estimates already slipping into late January online. The price of the first foldable iPhone reaches $3,199 at 2TB, creating a new tier above the Pro and Pro Max.Analysts say the Duo could boost Apple’s average selling prices through trade-ups, Android switchers and a halo effect across the rest of the iPhone lineup.In this article Apple's iPhone Duo, its most expensive iPhone ever, went up for preorder Friday, with launch-day pickup inventory selling out and some online delivery estimates already slipping into late January. The company said in a statement that the preorder demand was "nothing short of extraordinary." "We are working hard to get this revolutionary new product into customers' hands as quickly as possible, and we will continue accepting orders online," Apple said. Apple's first foldable phone starts at $1,999 and passes $3,000 at the 2TB storage tier. It is the biggest change to the physical design of the iPhone in years and establishes an entirely new price point above the Pro and Pro Max. The early rush offers a first glimpse at the demand behind Apple's bet: Whether a dramatic new design can persuade customers to spend more and push the iPhone even further as a status symbol. But analysts who spoke with CNBC said Apple's bet is not that foldables suddenly become a mass-market product. It is that a relatively small group of its highest-spending customers can become significantly more valuable. Foldables are expected to make up just over 2% of global smartphone units this year but nearly 7% of industry revenue, according to IDC. By 2030, IDC expects the category to account for 10% of smartphone revenue while still representing only about 3% of units. That gap between volume and value is central to Apple's opportunity. "Duo is fast becoming an aspirational foldable," IDC's Nabila Popal told CNBC, comparing its appeal with Apple's broader position as an aspirational smartphone brand. Popal, global senior research director for the Consumer Device Team at IDC, said the technology itself is not necessarily the breakthrough. Foldable Android phones have existed for years. What's new is Apple bringing that form factor to the enormous base of consumers already invested in the iPhone ecosystem. Apple itself has been exploring the form factor for more than a decade. In 2011, Ternus and five other Apple engineers filed a patent application for foldable electronic devices, according to a recent Time profile. "It's not that it's a breakthrough or new technology, but it's from Apple," Popal said. The Duo could also prove more accessible than some industry watchers had anticipated. Anshel Sag, an analyst at Moor Insights who attended Apple's launch event, said many expected the foldable iPhone to start between $2,400 and $2,500. Apple coming in at $1,999, Sag said, suggests the company "wants a lot of share." Sag expects the Duo to become "very much a status symbol" during the holiday season and potentially into next year. That status appeal could be reinforced by scarcity. Counterpoint Research Director Tarun Pathak told CNBC the firm expects initial demand to exceed supply. Apple has an installed base of roughly 1.4 billion iPhones, he noted, meaning even a small percentage of early adopters could overwhelm the roughly 6 million or fewer units Counterpoint expects to be available in the near term. IDC also expects supply to be constrained initially because of the complexity of the device and Apple's manufacturing and quality standards. "Exclusivity is part of the current appeal," Popal said. When the first Apple Watch launched, the company offered the 18-karat gold Edition starting at $10,000. Apple also formed a long-running partnership with Hermès around premium watch bands and designs. That push came during the tenure of Angela Ahrendts, the former Burberry CEO who joined Apple in 2014 to lead retail and online stores, as the company experimented with bringing more of the language and presentation of luxury fashion into its stores and products. The Duo takes that idea into Apple's largest product business. IDC expects Apple to ship roughly 7 million units this year, or roughly 3% of Apple's total shipments in 2026.Popal, the IDC analyst, forecasts Duo shipments could grow another 70% next year. That would give Apple roughly 40% of the global foldable market and would make it the category's largest player, surpassing Samsung and Huawei. According to her forecast, Apple could ship as many Duos in the next six months as the previous category leaders did in all of 2025. But the more important number for Apple may not be units. A large share of Duo customers are expected to be existing iPhone owners, analysts said, including consumers who otherwise might have purchased a Pro Max and are now trading up to a device costing hundreds of dollars more. Others could add the Duo as a second smartphone, with Apple's ecosystem allowing users to move relatively seamlessly between it and their primary iPhone. Popal said that migration from roughly $1,200 premium iPhones to a device starting at nearly $2,000 should provide a "healthy boost" to Apple's revenue even if overall volumes remain relatively small. The bank expects the Duo to have a disproportionate impact on iPhone revenue because of its much higher average selling price, even as overall iPhone shipments are expected to remain roughly flat next year. JPMorgan said the iPhone 18 cycle is increasingly likely to be driven by price and product mix rather than unit growth. D.A. Davidson analyst Gil Luria said Apple needs the Duo to succeed as it comes up against a difficult set of earnings comps with its strongest upgrade cycle in years. "Without an uplift from Duo, they may experience some pretty pedestrian revenue growth," Luria told CNBC. The device gives Apple several ways to generate that uplift, he added. It raises the company's average selling price by capturing die-hard Apple customers who might otherwise have bought a Pro Max. It could bring in some consumers who previously bought folding Android phones because Apple did not offer one. And it could create a halo around the rest of the iPhone lineup. Luria said some consumers will visit Apple stores specifically to see the Duo, "but probably walk out with an iPhone or iPhone Pro at half the price." That means the Duo can potentially help Apple even when someone decides not to buy it. Lead times for the iPhone 18 Pro have softened in several markets compared with the prior cycle, while the more expensive Pro Max has held up better, according to JPMorgan's tracking. Morgan Stanley has separately said its supply-chain checks are consistent with unusually early component order reductions for the Pro and Pro Max, though the firm has not yet seen evidence that those adjustments have translated into cuts to finished iPhone production. That puts more pressure on the Duo to pull buyers toward the very top of Apple's lineup. Apple's move toward a more expensive iPhone comes as the economics of the broader smartphone market become increasingly difficult. Consumers are already holding on to phones for longer, and global smartphone growth is slowing. Wayne Lam, an analyst at TechInsights, said moving the iPhone further upmarket gives Apple another way to protect the revenue generated by its most important product. "Given that the iPhone is almost 20 years old, there really isn't anywhere else to head to, given Apple's market position," Lam told CNBC. With smartphone sales expected to slow, he said, "moving upmarket allows Apple to maintain the all-important iPhone revenues they report every quarter." Lam described the Duo as an aspirational or luxury product rather than something designed for the average consumer. But unlike Apple's Vision products, he believes the foldable phone has a path toward becoming a larger category over time, particularly as artificial intelligence changes how consumers interact with their devices. The trade-off is that pushing prices higher could also make consumers wait longer to upgrade. Higher iPhone prices could stretch already-long upgrade cycles even further, Lam said, creating what he described as a potential negative feedback loop: devices become more expensive, consumers hold on to them longer and overall demand falls. Still, Lam expects demand for the Duo to be high relative to its initially limited supply and said the device could "set the bar for premium iPhones moving forward." articles.title: AI-Generated CSAM Exposes New Jersey Prosecutor
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav New Jersey’s deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, was arrested on “felony charges related to AI-generated child sexual abuse material (CSAM),” Bucks County Detectives said in a press release Thursday. In the US, cops have vowed to crack down on AI CSAM since at least 2024, when the Department of Justice made one of the earliest arrests . After charging a Wisconsin man with spreading “thousands of realistic images of prepubescent minors” across Telegram and Instagram, the DOJ clarified to law enforcement that “CSAM generated by AI is still CSAM.” New Jersey’s deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, was arrested at his home Thursday. Credit: via Bucks County Detectives New Jersey’s deputy attorney general, Brian Richard Fitzgerald, was arrested at his home Thursday. Credit: via Bucks County Detectives On Thursday, New Jersey officials accused 51-year-old Fitzgerald of using AI to make photos from social media of real minors into sexualized images that he then distributed on social media. Fitzgerald was charged after the National Center for Missing and Exploited Children received a tip that a Discord user shared an illicit image in July. Cops then used “digital forensics and subscriber records” linked to the Discord account and “associated Internet protocol addresses” to track the user to Fitzgerald’s home address. After a search Thursday, cops “recovered prompts and scripts used to create artificially generated child sexual abuse material using an AI program,” the press release said. They also found Discord chat logs where Fitzgerald, under the Discord username “thegentlemanpervert_2160_07833,” allegedly “admitted to making multiple illicit images using artificial intelligence and sharing them with other users.” Fitzgerald’s is a rare case where an official employed by the state’s top law enforcement and legal office has been accused of making and distributing AI CSAM, although some cops have been arrested for the crime. Earlier this year, a Pennsylvania cop was arrested for making AI porn from photos on driver’s licenses , and more recently in Korea, a police officer was arrested for making AI porn, including CSAM, The Korea Times reported . In New Jersey, the deputy attorney general has been charged with possession of CSAM, dissemination of photos or film of CSAM, and “criminal use of a communication facility,” detectives said. According to his LinkedIn, Fitzgerald had served as deputy attorney general since 2016, preparing insurance fraud and insurance licensee cases for trial as a state prosecutor. New Jersey’s district attorney, Joe Khan, said in a statement that New Jersey is aligned with the DOJ in viewing AI CSAM as being as harmful as CSAM. “No one is above the law, least of all someone entrusted with upholding it,” Khan said. “Our office will pursue these cases aggressively and hold offenders fully accountable, regardless of their profession or title.” Ashley Belanger Senior Policy Reporter Ashley Belanger Senior Policy Reporter 37 Comments

articles.title: Nigerian Electricity Theft Crackdown Faces Data Problem
articles.content: By Nicola Mawson , Contributing journalist Johannesburg, 16 Oct 2026 City Power wants a platform to monitor prepaid electricity purchases in near-real-time. (Graphic: Nicola Mawson | Pexels) City Power’s R3.96 billion in non-technical electricity losses is the target of a tender for near-real-time monitoring of prepaid purchases, but experts warn analytics will flag suspects, not recover money. According to City Power’s latest annual report , the 2024/25 figure was up from R3.45 billion the previous year. It accounted for 20.85% of electricity purchased and included theft , illegal connections, meter bypassing, faulty equipment and billing errors. The report also shows City Power has already introduced automated meter management, targeted audits and customer database reconciliation to address non-technical losses. City Power reported auditing 40 000 customers who had converted to prepaid electricity but were not purchasing tokens. At the end of June 2025, prepaid customers represented approximately 74% of its customer base of 396 461 but accounted for just 11% of revenue. According to June 2026 technical specifications for a tender advertised this month, City Power wants a platform to monitor prepaid electricity purchases in near-real-time. The tender covers third-party prepaid vending, revenue enhancement, customer monitoring, meter audits and advanced metering infrastructure support, and successful bidders must integrate their technology into City Power’s existing systems. The documents also require that the appointed providers maintain 99.5% system availability. All customer and transaction data will remain City Power’s property, the document states. City Power says bidders must be able to identify revenue leakage. (Source: City Power tender document) City Power says bidders must be able to identify revenue leakage, suspected theft, meter tampering, illegal connections, bypass conditions and other non-technical losses. Service providers must also identify customers with abnormal behaviour, such as low purchases, zero vending, declining consumption or irregular vending patterns, and recommend interventions. Bidders may propose artificial intelligence (AI) for anomaly detection, theft prediction, revenue forecasting, predictive maintenance and customer risk scoring. However, City Power requires AI outputs to be transparent, explainable, auditable and compliant with the Protection of Personal Information Act, with human decision-making retained. Jacqui Muller, a researcher at Belgium Campus iTversity and a PhD candidate in computer science and information technology, warns that the proposed monitoring capabilities depend on the type of electricity meters installed. “Standard prepaid meters are essentially one-way. You see the token sale, not the consumption,” Muller says. Near-real-time monitoring needs smart meters with reliable communications, a system that can take in interval readings, and clean links between the vending, billing, meter and GIS systems, she adds. At the end of June 2025, prepaid customers represented approximately 74% of City Power’s customer base of 396 461, but accounted for just 11% of revenue. (Image redrawn by GenAI) Muller notes that, without these, real-time “really means real-time sales data”. A decline in electricity purchases could indicate theft, but could also reflect a faulty meter, an empty property, the installation of solar or backup power, or customers purchasing electricity in bulk, says Muller. “Analytics is good at spotting that something is unusual. It’s poor at explaining why,” Muller says. “The model produces a list of suspects. The answer only comes from a physical meter audit and checking the customer’s records,” she adds. Mark Walker, director and co-founder of T4i, also cautions that the effectiveness of automated detection depends on the quality, reliability and frequency of the data flowing from the meters. AI could generate unreliable predictions when data is poor or incomplete, Walker says, while integrating new technology with existing electricity infrastructure presents risks involving outdated meters, incompatible systems, budget overruns and shortages of technical skills. “Garbage in, garbage out rules still apply and are paramount,” he says. City Power reported auditing 40 000 customers in 2024/25 who had converted to prepaid electricity but were not purchasing tokens. (Image redrawn by GenAI) Muller also notes: “If past audits mostly targeted certain areas, the model will keep pointing back at those areas.” Bidders should be asked to report false-positive rates from field-verified outcomes, not just detection rates, she says. Research published in August 2026 by Cape Peninsula University of Technology academics, who reviewed 90 studies published between 2015 and 2025, found that while machine learning shows promise in detecting electricity theft, evidence of its effectiveness in real-world deployments remains limited. They identified challenges including insufficient verified theft data, false positives and difficulties applying models across different electricity networks. Walker says the technology could theoretically cut non-technical losses, but illegal connections, incomplete data and municipal enforcement inertia mean the benefit would need to be weighed against the cost of the system. Analytics could help City Power target inspections more effectively, says Muller. “Analytics doesn’t recover money. Inspections, prosecutions, reconnection policy and community trust do,” she says. “Much non-technical loss is illegal connections in areas with no account to analyse,” Muller adds. She warns that detailed purchasing and consumption patterns can reveal household circumstances, including when properties are unoccupied, raising privacy concerns. “A risk score should only ever trigger a physical inspection, never a disconnection.” She adds that customers must be able to challenge adverse findings. Muller also warns that the models and the logic linking the systems could belong to up to five vendors, so City Power may not be able to explain or reproduce a decision once a contract ends. City Power should insist on independent model audits and verified recovery figures and should not reward suppliers for generating alerts or pay the firm that scores the risk per disconnection or per rand recovered on the same case, says Muller. “Fix the data before buying the AI.” See also City Power ‘making progress’ with billing issues Joburg flags financial risk, but claims ‘accurate’ bills Share

articles.title: Utah AI Sandbox Launches Healthcare Pilots, Raises Questions
articles.content: Stay Connected Featured eBooks Health Technology: Relaunch of VA EHR Read Now Law Enforcement Technology Read Now Insights & Reports By Christian Robles , Technology Reporter, Nextgov/FCW | October 16, 2026 03:50 PM ET The state is mulling how the high-profile AI initiative will tackle medical liability concerns, independent third-party analysis and other questions. State and Local Health Tech FDA Regulations SANTA FE, N.M. — Utah announced three new pilots last week to test artificial intelligence capabilities that can refill chronic condition-related prescriptions, write initial acne prescriptions and offer virtual physical therapy, but a regulator acknowledged the state still has key questions to address as the model scales nationwide. Utah regulators have “evidentiary standards, [and we are] working on governance guidance. We're working on a liability bill to begin building the statutory framework around” its AI sandbox, Zach Boyd, director of Utah’s Office of Artificial Intelligence Policy — or OAIP — said at the ADAPT conference in Santa Fe, New Mexico on Thursday. Through the AI sandbox, Utah has allowed companies to test new technologies in exchange for regulatory relief and state oversight. Utah started AI pilots in 2024 with a mental health support app , but the sandbox did not garner national attention until this year, as the state allowed AI to refill certain prescriptions with clinician oversight through a pilot with health technology company Doctronic. The Utah Medical Licensing Board fiercely opposed that effort, calling for an immediate suspension of it in an April letter to the Utah Department of Commerce and criticizing the state for not consulting them. “We hit a nerve,” Boyd said. The Utah Medical Licensing Board has since formed a working group that meets with state regulators once a week, he explained, adding that the détente came from six months of discussions and updates to the AI pilot. In an interview with Nextgov/FCW , Boyd noted that Utah removed some drugs from the list of prescriptions AI can refill following scrutiny from the Utah Medical Licensing Board. The list of 190 drugs dropped headache reliever Butalbital and antiarrhythmic medication Flecainide, according to OAIP. But Utah regulators are still mulling over how the state should split legal liability between AI and the human clinicians who oversee them if patients are harmed. Regulators have interpreted the law to mean that the AI sandbox does not have authority to change liability rules, but they have pulled several short-term levers to address the question, Boyd explained. OAIP has required Doctronic and AI pilot companies that have engaged with the sandbox since then to carry special liability insurance and not waive liability. However, “in the long run, we think [insurance is] less sustainable, and we need a way to hold the vendor directly liable for the actions of their automated system,” Boyd said, adding that regulators expect the default is that physicians will bear too much liability. Boyd hopes the state will unveil a liability bill this month or next month during Utah’s interim legislative session. The bill will kick off a “multi-year process” to refine liability, he said. Another big question facing Utah’s sandbox is whether the Food and Drug Administration will regulate pilot AI technology. The FDA generally requires software that treats or diagnoses patients to undergo pre-market authorization, which some lawyers told STAT could include the pilot AI technology like Doctronic’s AI prescription refiller. The FDA has so far been silent on the Utah experiment. Boyd declined to speak for the FDA but said he hopes to work with federal regulators on creating a unified regulatory pathway for AI. “It’s really appealing to people to have kind of a vet once, deployed everywhere, aggregate oversight across jurisdictions” model, Boyd told ADAPT attendees. “A model like that feeds nicely into the federal government and the kind of oversight that they’ll also want to exercise,” he added. Utah has tapped six independent evaluators to assess AI companies’ technical claims and share results with the state. They include the Coalition for Health AI, Clarion AI Partners, Glacis Technologies, mpathic AI, Vega Health and Stanford Clinical Excellence Research Center. Much like with liability, there are question marks about the independent evaluators. Utah spelled out the general expectations for health care software piloted through the state’s AI sandbox. The technical document says those technologies should account for managing AI input uncertainty, clinical context, patients’ emotional intelligence and other factors throughout its pilot. “Half of [the document] is probably wrong, but it's definitely, it's got to be, about the most mature thing that exists,” Boyd told ADAPT attendees. With those expectations, future AI pilots will have to contract with an independent evaluator, Boyd said. The data evaluators will assess will depend on the specific AI pilot’s intended application, patient population, outcomes and specifications, Mark Sendak, CEO and co-founder of Vega Health, told Nextgov/FCW . The startup would work with the state and the pilot company on crafting the appropriate data analysis while bringing in external partners with the necessary expertise to assess specific pilots, he said. But because AI models often change over time and will expand to serve new patient populations, Sendak expects independent evaluators to constantly repeat assessments and share that data with the state. Utah has also signed master agreements with health systems Intermountain Health and University of Utah Health, allowing them to pitch AI pilots that the state can approve. “One of the underrated advantages of a sandbox is it helps the regulator learn so much,” Boyd told ADAPT attendees. However, the initiative proceeds with substantial unanswered questions regarding scalability, long-term regulatory integration, and potential ethical pitfalls, underscoring the experimental and often uncertain nature of balancing innovation with responsible governance in the rapidly evolving AI landscape.

The company will license the platform architecture, implementation methodologies and operational expertise that enabled Abu Dhabi to build and operate TAMM at scale. By combining pre-built capabilities with proven implementation methods and operating practices refined through millions of real-world interactions, TAMM Global can help governments accelerate deployment without having to build an equivalent platform from scratch. articles.title: OpenAI Models Hacked Crypto Wallet, Breached Websites
articles.content: Text settings Story text Size Small Standard Large Width * Standard Wide Links Standard Orange * Subscribers only    Learn more Minimize to nav OpenAI said internal models hacked two more websites, bypassed company-imposed browsing restrictions, and used exposed credentials to draw cryptocurrency from a wallet it couldn’t otherwise access, in the latest installment of disclosures of its agents performing unethical and likely illegal acts. The company on Thursday issued reports of four new incidents, all of which occurred in June. They come after the company revealed in July that internal test agents exploited a zero-day vulnerability in a tool designed to restrict their access to the Internet. They then broke into the network of AI tool provider Hugging Face. The agents took that illegal action to steal answers to a hacking test that weren’t available when completing the tasks on their own. The incident—which likely would have resulted in criminal charges had they been performed directly by a person—has further heightened concerns that widespread AI use could have harmful effects on an unprecedented scale. Easier to beg for forgiveness than ask permission In two of the cases reported Thursday, OpenAI agents tasked with retrieving information from websites hacked them when the models ran into obstacles obtaining it directly. In one incident during reinforcement training, a model that received access denials when trying to retrieve historical hospital-bed statistics on a government statistics website “used the site’s file-download feature to retrieve server configuration and application files, including sensitive credentials,” OpenAI said . “It inspected the application code, bypassed the statistics endpoint’s authorization checks, and retrieved data that had previously been denied. The model saved the data locally.” In the other incident , a model instructed to retrieve figures from a public research dashboard bypassed the organization’s security controls and used the unauthorized access to steal credentials. It then made configuration changes on the server. In one evaluation, the changes let the model make an internal search tool relay queries to the public dashboard. In a second evaluation, the model downloaded five non-public tables containing 147,451 rows. OpenAI researchers had prompted the agents to retrieve only five dashboard figures. Even after resetting the setting, the model continued using the token to retrieve non-public data. “The evaluation ended without the model disclosing that it had guessed answers, accessed the organization’s internal systems, downloaded non-public tables, or changed the authentication configuration,” OpenAI said. “All five answers in this evaluation were marked incorrect.” In a third report , the company said a model prompted to update a cryptocurrency trading application used funds from a locked wallet on a test network. The model “derived wallet keys from publicly known developer recovery phrases, found an account with test-network funds, and used that account to pay for the requested contract deployment.” The report continued: “The model questioned whether it had permission, then reasoned that a public recovery phrase and valueless test-network tokens made the funds acceptable to use. The deployment succeeded and charged transaction fees to the account. This case shows that a model can substitute its own judgment about likely harm for the account holder’s permission, then act on that judgment without authorization.” In the last report , OpenAI said that a model bypassed restrictions researchers had placed on the types of web requests it could make. During reinforcement-learning training, the model had been prompted to seek public trade statistics. OpenAI went on: After finding a public yearbook and submitting an answer, it continued probing for another route to the statistics service. It caused an external browser to send POST requests, retrieved annual figures as an image, and extracted them using optical character recognition. It then developed a reusable helper that returned response text through a forwarding service and callback mailbox, repeatedly checked the retrieved figures, and used saved data in submitted responses. This case shows how a model can bypass restrictions on its own tools by getting external services to perform the blocked actions, even after finding another way to answer the question. The model first tried to use an external browser with permission to make GET requests on its behalf, then used JavaScript to obtain the information. The model then used an online mailbox to troubleshoot the technique. Eventually, the model settled on a different method: It asked the external browser to open a web form that sent the trade query to the statistics service by POST. When the browser displayed the response, a rendering service returned a GIF image of the page. The model then used optical character recognition to read the figures from the image. It has become common for researchers and journalists to describe incidents like these as AI “going rogue.” That’s not necessarily true. While prompts fed to the models didn’t instruct them to use the alternate methods for completing their objectives, models are trained to be efficient, steadfastly persistent, and, when possible, to find shortcuts that lessen workloads. Further, most or all of the models had disabled certain guardrails that might have prevented the actions. In this sense, the models performed precisely as OpenAI had trained them to. Justice Marco Aurelio Bellizze ruled that Meta cannot reduce the distribution of political content, restrict searches or remove posts in a way that creates an imbalance between Lula and Bolsonaro. His ruling also orders the company to ensure its artificial intelligence tool applies identical criteria to both candidacies. Bellizze said in his ruling that Meta must pay a fine of 500,000 reais ($98,700) per day if it fails to comply. articles.title: AOC Transfers $1M to Michigan Progressive Candidate
articles.content: xwhatsapp-strokecopylinkgoogleAdd Al Jazeera on GoogleinfoUS Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez addresses the crowd during a campaign rally for Michigan Democratic US Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed [File: Jose Juarez/The Associated Press]By Al Jazeera Staff16 Oct 2026United States Representative Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez has transferred $1m to support Michigan Senate candidate Abdul El-Sayed, in a major progressive push for the upstart politician. Ocasio-Cortez, who has become a progressive stalwart since her surprise 2018 congressional victory, confirmed the donation in a statement on Friday and a speech in Michigan. The transfer was first reported by the New York Times. The lawmaker pointed to political attacks against El-Sayed, a large portion of which have focused on his Muslim faith, his Egyptian heritage and support for Palestine. “I’m not waking up on November 4th wishing I did more to combat the smears aimed at Abdul,” Ocasio-Cortez said in a statement, in reference to the November 3 congressional midterm election. “I’m leaving everything I can on the field.” Speaking at an event in the Detroit area, Ocasio added that she transferred the money from her own campaign to show “the cavalry is coming”. “And the only reason I’m doing that is because I see the energy of each and every one of you stepping up to make an effort,” she said. The move comes as Ocasio-Cortez has been campaigning for El-Sayed in Michigan, joining him on a bus tour of the conservative-leaning Upper Peninsula area before hosting three events on Friday in the state’s largest city, Detroit. El Sayed’s populist progressive message has gained traction with voters in the state, where he currently leads Republican Mike Rogers by 2.6 percentage points, according to a Real Clear Politics average of high-quality polls. The support from Ocasio Cortez, who is weighing a potential 2028 presidential candidacy, also underscores a wider effort by progressives to court disaffected Trump voters. The pair highlighted economic issues while on the trail in the midwestern state. Trump’s approval ratings are at a career low ahead of the midterm vote. A slate of recent polls has shown widespread public disapproval of Trump’s handling of the US economy and the knock-on effects of the US-Israeli war on Iran. Recent polls have also shown an appetite for a more comprehensive change in US government, signalling a potential opening for candidates running outside of the establishment of both major parties. An AP-NORC poll released this week found that 80 percent of respondents said they supported either a “complete and total upheaval” or “substantial change” in how the country is run. Speaking alongside Ocasio-Cortez on Friday, progressive House Representative Ayanna Pressley called on the Democratic Senatorial Campaign Committee, which raises and allocates funds for Senate candidates, to make “an equitable investment in progressive and diverse candidates” like El-Sayed, Florida Senate candidate Angie Nixon and Mississippi Senate candidate Scott Colom. El-Sayed, who received an early endorsement from progressive US Senator Bernie Sanders of Vermont, has also recently been embraced by a handful of more centrist Democrats, including former President Barack Obama and former Vice President Kamala Harris. Sanders donated $250,000 to El-Sayed’s campaign, CNN reports. The new financial support from Ocasio-Cortez, which was given to the Abdul for Michigan Victory Fund, arrived as the Michigan Senate race has become one of the most expensive in the state’s history, topping $268m as of October 15, according to the Detroit Free Press. El-Sayed, meanwhile, outpaced Rogers in fundraising from July 1 to September 30, bringing in $30.6m compared to Rogers’ $9.6m. Still, Rogers’ campaign had more cash on hand as of September 30, with $6.5m compared to El-Sayed’s $3.8 million. Michigan is among the key Senate races that could determine control of the chamber for the final two years of US President Donald Trump’s term. Republicans currently hold 53 seats in the 100-member body.

articles.title: Hacker News: Claude Code Team's Code Review
articles.content: EngineeringHow the Claude Code team does code reviewHow do you review code at the volume agents produce it? On the Claude Code team, once we had high coverage and deep reviews, we started optimizing for the minimum amount of human review time that doesn't raise reverts or incidents. We've said before that Claude writes about 90 percent of Claude Code's own code. So how do we review code at the volume we produce it? Does anyone read code anymore? And if something breaks, who catches it? This post covers the code review flow on the Claude Code team and how it has evolved. From June to September, merged pull requests to Claude Code's codebase more than doubled while the share that had to be reverted fell by more than 40 percent. We didn't remove review. But we did move most of the reading to machines, optimized for human time and attention, and invested heavily in making it fast and easy to undo mistakes. When agents write code, the number of changes goes up, fast. In Anthropic's monorepo, changes landing per day went from about 2,500 in May to more than 30,000 in September this year. Claude Code lives in its own repository, separate from the monorepo, but it's seeing a lot of pressure too. When you are shipping this fast, manual, line-by-line code review is incredibly difficult if not impossible. This article mainly focuses on finding and fixing issues, but we will come back to the second job near the end. We think "did a human read the code?" is an imprecise proxy for "what could go wrong with this change, and which check—automated or human—is the right one to catch it?" Asking that question also changed when review happens. Before, review was a gate at the end of the road: write the code, open a PR, wait for your colleague. Now, review runs continuously, more like spellcheck while you write. Most changes have been reviewed and fixed by Claude at least once before a human is asked to look. This catches most routine mistakes, and saves team attention for higher-level questions and scrutiny. We want to preserve human time and attention for issues only humans can solve and make sure automated checks catch the rest. At our current rate of change, there is still an incredible amount of work for humans to do, and our team encounters new and novel challenges almost daily. Human time covers both sides of review's cost: the time people spend reviewing, and the time they spend fixing what bad code breaks. Cutting the first doesn't help if the time just shows up in the second. So the goal is that most pull requests in the Claude Code repos (the CLI, the desktop and web apps, and the mobile apps) merge with at most one human in the loop, who can be the author, with no increase in reverts or incidents. To measure human time, we track human approvals per PR (median and 95th percentile), human comments, and how long a PR waits on a person. Revert and incident rates are the guardrail: if they rise, we haven't saved human time, we've only moved it. A typical change, from an engineer's laptop (or a Claude session in Slack), goes through multiple layers of code review. Few get through all of them, and rollback handles the rest. 1. The work is verified before anyone else looks Most review now happens before a PR exists. We give Claude something it can run—like tests, a build or a screenshot to compare against the design—and ask it to show the output instead of saying it's done. Then a subagent reviews the diff with fresh context. Both habits come from our best-practices guide. Before opening a PR, many of us also run a few internal skills: one hunts for bugs, one simplifies the diff, and one checks the behavior end to end. UI changes also get checked against our design guidelines. Boris Cherny, who created Claude Code, has called giving Claude a way to verify its work probably the most important thing for getting good results. He estimates it makes the final result two to three times better, and writes, "Verification looks different for each domain. It might be as simple as running a bash command, or running a test suite, or testing the app in a browser or phone simulator." When the automated reviewer keeps flagging the same thing, we fix it at the source: in the skill, with a lint rule, or with updates to instructional files such as: Every pull request gets a Claude review before a person looks. It reads the diff against the whole repo and the PR's stated intent, and asks: does the change solve its problem, fit the system, or break something else? On a bug fix, it looks for the root cause. The public version, Code Review for Claude Code, is now generally available on Team and Enterprise plans, and /code-review runs a lighter version locally. When we launched the research preview, the share of internal PRs getting substantive review comments went from 16% to 54%. Most PRs over 1,000 lines get findings, and most small ones come back clean. Admins set each repo to Quick, Standard, or Deep. Deep is worth it where one missed bug costs more than the extra review time. Findings get verified by other agents before humans review them. Several agents look for bugs at the same time. Then a separate group votes on each finding, and it only gets posted if enough of them agree it's real. Findings that are only about style, diagnostics, or cleanup get dropped. We A/B tested those filters on our own PRs before keeping them. What's left shows up as inline comments sorted by severity. Each is tagged Important, Nit, or Pre-existing, so a bug the PR didn't introduce doesn't look like the author's fault. Every finding has to be answered. You either fix it or resolve the thread with a reason. Often an agent picks up the fix overnight, so the author comes back to a PR that's already been through another round. Security gets its own automated review too. A PR can't merge while any finding from the bug review or the security review is still open. You either fix it or close the thread with a short reason, which is how you clear a false positive. If a later commit fixes the issue, the finding clears on its own. You can set up the same thing with the open-source security review GitHub Action or the /security-review command. Setup is covered in automated security reviews in Claude Code. The usual: lint, type checks, tests on every platform, and a build. (We wrote about scaling CI for this volume here.) A typical CLI pull request may run dozens of checks before anyone looks at it. The PR template asks how the change was tested and how to undo it. Claude can fill that in, but the person who asked for the change signs off on it. A docs fix and an auto-updater change carry different risk, so they get different review. The change sets the tier, not the author. A classifier reads the change and picks its risk tier. A second classifier asks whether this particular change needs another person even when its tier says it doesn't. Some paths always need a person, anything owners have listed as sensitive and any CI workflow file. Only trusted authors get the lighter paths. Only authors on the repo's trusted list get the lighter paths, mostly the team that owns it. Everyone else needs a second person to approve. An agent's approval never counts as a person's, either. Automated review can clear a low-risk change, but it can't fill a slot that calls for a human. Whoever prompted the change is on the hook for it. On an agent-written PR, the person directing the agent counts as one of the required reviewers, the same as if they'd typed the code themselves. An approval covers one specific commit. If new commits land that the system can't vouch for, like an agent's push or a merge someone resolved by hand, the approval has to be given again. The merge queue re-runs every check against main with the change applied, so two PRs that pass separately can't combine into a broken main. New behavior usually ships behind a flag to Anthropic employees first, and our heavy use often surfaces regressions before users do. Public releases go to the latest channel first. The stable channel trails it. Some mistakes will still get through, so the last layer is about catching them fast. Flags turn off without a deploy. Claude Code has a weekly on-call rotation, and incident reviews ask which layer should have caught the issue. Noticing a bad merge still depends on the author and on-call as well as the revert and incident dashboards. We don't yet have circuit breakers that tighten approval when those numbers move; engineers here want them before more code moves to zero-human merges. One colleague said slowing down does lower your error rate, but mostly because you're doing less of everything. We'd rather get faster at noticing and fixing problems. Our code review process is constantly improving in a loop. Any incidents are now an eval. The team collected past PRs that caused incidents, with their fix-forwards and reverts, and had engineers who know that code confirm each bug and where it lived. The reviewer runs against that set daily. next change Incident or revert a change that broke something Expert-checked case experts confirm the bug Added to the set each incident adds a case Daily eval run scored against every case Score went up? keep it; if not, drop it Change the reviewer its prompts, tools or model FIG CThe eval grows with every incident, and every change to the reviewer is scored against all of it. We measure noise by watching what people do with the comments. It's easy to catch more bugs if you don't mind flagging a lot of non-bugs, so we need a check on that. We sort every comment the reviewer leaves by how the person on the PR responded: they fixed it, said it was wrong, said the behavior was intentional, or decided it didn't matter. We also run the reviewer on PRs we know are clean and count how often it reports something that would have led someone to make a harmful change. Our priority, written down, is catching real bugs first and cutting review rounds second. Noise costs more when the author is an agent. A person can wave off a nit in seconds. An agent fixes it, which means another commit and another round of review. Review has to converge. An agent author and an agent reviewer can keep each other busy indefinitely. One CLI PR went through more than fifty rounds of review and fixes overnight before its author stopped it. When we ran git blame on what the reviewer kept flagging, about 59% of it was code that had been there since the reviewer's first pass. The reviewer was rarely finding new bugs, it was finding a few more old ones each round. We made it worse ourselves. We'd gotten used to running several rounds by default, since each pass catches something new. This can be worthwhile on a risky change, but not on every PR. The team now tracks rounds-to-pass alongside recall, and changed re-review: Review agents also run nightly over existing code, helping us catch old bugs before they show up somewhere else. Need five or more rounds 8.9% 1.5% Mean reviews to pass 2.08 1.32 before after the convergence work Pass after one review and fix round 65% 78% Need five or more rounds 8.9% 1.5% Mean reviews to pass 2.08 1.32 before after the convergence work FIG DFewer review rounds per internal pull request after the convergence changes WHERE HUMANS STAY IN THE LOOP Pulling a senior engineer out of deep work to catch a routine mistake costs far more than an automated review. At Anthropic, our jobs have moved from reading every diff to the decisions machines are bad at: Should we build it? Risky code Architecture Reading the evidence Owning the outcome an automated check a person decides FIG EPeople moved from reading every diff to the decisions machines are bad at SHARING CONTEXT ACROSS THE TEAM Code review's second job has always been to spread codebase understanding. Reading a teammate's diff is how you learn what changed and how the pieces fit. If machines do most of the reading, how does anyone learn the code? We don't have a formal process for this. Nobody on the team keeps a complete mental model of Claude Code in their head, and we don't think anyone needs to. When someone wants to understand a part of the codebase, they ask Claude to write an explainer for exactly that slice. It takes minutes and reflects the code as it is today. Some of us go a step further and have Claude build a small artifact that visualizes that part of the code and teaches it the way that person likes to learn. If the goal is to spend human attention well, this beats reading trivial diffs line by line. A one-line copy change teaches you almost nothing. An explainer for the module you're about to change teaches you a lot. Our culture of defaulting to working on open Slack channels helps too, since you see what others are building while they build it. If you land a small or medium change and something still goes wrong, it's a team norm that you usually fix it. A few things keep this from going badly: Ownership is also shared. Much of the team works in open channels where anyone can see what others are building, pick up a thread, or point a Claude at a gap, and feedback comes from people who don't own the code too. That openness is a big part of how quality stays high without a gate on every line. Agents make it cheap to start things, so some work shouldn't land. Usually someone in the channel asks why, points at an earlier decision, or suggests a simpler route, and the author closes or reshapes the PR. Since the code was fast to write, closing the PR doesn't feel like a loss. The trick is to raise a different direction in the thread early, not as a blocking comment on a finished PR. Most of the pieces to do this with your team exist today. Code Review's announcement said approving a pull request is still a human call; the product posts findings, not approvals. Our own repos go further, letting owners decide which low-risk changes merge on automated checks alone, and that line keeps moving. When a review misses something, we ask what the model didn't have in front of it and put the fix into a CLAUDE.md, a skill or a new check. The goal hasn't changed: less human time per change, and no more reverts than before. If your team lets agents open pull requests, we'd like to hear which checks you've automated, which still need a person, and what you think we have wrong.
